sections.overview: Acanthoscurria geniculata is a large, ground-dwelling tarantula native to Brazil. Its dark body and striking pale bands at the leg joints make it easy to recognize as the Brazilian whiteknee. It is a member of the New World tarantula family Theraphosidae and is frequently studied in laboratory work on spider development, although many details of its behaviour in the wild remain poorly documented.
sections.identification: The spider is robust and hairy, with a dark brown to nearly black body and conspicuous white to cream bands around the leg joints; reddish or pinkish hairs may show on the abdomen. It has four pairs of walking legs, as do other spiders. Care references commonly describe mature females as larger or heavier than males, but no dependable species-specific measurements quantify this difference. Commonly cited adult dimensions are about 8–10 cm body length and an 18–20 cm diagonal leg span; these figures come mainly from care references rather than standardized wild morphometric surveys. No dependable body height, width or mass range was located. The white joint bands are the clearest field mark; do not identify it from size alone, since several large Brazilian tarantulas can look similar.
sections.habitat: Museum specimen records place the species in Brazil, including Pará, Roraima, Rondônia and Mato Grosso. The Cincinnati Zoo describes its habitat as rainforest in the Amazon Basin. As a terrestrial tarantula it is associated with the forest floor, but detailed field studies of its natural burrows, seasonal habitat use and microclimate are scarce; captive enclosures should not be mistaken for field evidence.
sections.diet: Like other tarantulas, it is a predatory spider that captures animal prey and subdues it with its fangs and venom. The Cincinnati Zoo lists insects, lizards and small mammals in its diet, but the proportions of these prey in the wild have not been established. A precise species-specific field diet should therefore not be inferred from a captive menu.
sections.behavior: It hunts from the ground and can seize prey with a quick lunge. Like other New World tarantulas, it possesses urticating abdominal setae that it can brush or flick toward a threat; these hairs can irritate skin and especially the eyes. A defensive bite is also possible, so the animal should not be handled. The species' notoriety in captivity does not provide a reliable measure of how often it is exposed or active in the forest.
sections.reproduction: The female makes and guards an egg sac. A Cincinnati Zoo species account reports 50–200 eggs in a sac, while a laboratory embryology paper documented one cocoon containing about 2,000 eggs; the difference shows that clutch counts vary and depend on the individual and conditions. The laboratory study describes embryos and cocoons but does not establish a typical wild clutch size or reproductive season.
sections.ecology: As a large ground predator, it forms part of the invertebrate food web of Brazilian rainforest. Its exact prey spectrum, natural predators and effects on local populations have not been quantified in the sources reviewed. Museum records and captive popularity are much more extensive than direct ecological studies, so claims about its abundance or ecosystem role should remain modest.
sections.conservation: The sources reviewed do not provide a current IUCN assessment, population trend or quantitative conservation status for Acanthoscurria geniculata. Its occurrence in museum collections and the pet trade is not evidence that wild populations are secure. More field data would be needed to assess range, abundance and any local threats.
